claim: Lung disease causes significant morbidity and mortality, and is exacerbated by environmental injury, for example through lipopolysaccharide (LPS) or ozone (O3).
source: Lung disease causes significant morbidity and mortality, and is exacerbated by environmental injury, for example through lipopolysaccharide (LPS) or ozone (O3).
evidence: This is a general statement about lung disease that draws from established medical knowledge and is supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: TLR4, the prototypic receptor for LPS, also mediates inflammation after O3, triggered by endogenous hyaluronan.
source: TLR4, the prototypic receptor for LPS, also mediates inflammation after O3, triggered by endogenous hyaluronan.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Garantziotis et al., 2010; Garantziotis et al., 2009) as referenced in the abstract and introduction.

claim: TLR5, the flagellin receptor, is expressed in alveolar macrophages.
source: TLR5, the flagellin receptor, is expressed in alveolar macrophages, and regulates immune responses to environmental injury.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Shikhagaie et al., 2014 in the introduction.

claim: TLR5 impacts the in vivo response to LPS, hyaluronan and O3.
source: Using in vivo animal models of TLR4-mediated inflammations (LPS, O3, hyaluronan), we show that TLR5 impacts the in vivo response to LPS, hyaluronan and O3.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from in vivo animal models presented in Figures 1, 2, and 3.

claim: Immune cells of human carriers of a dominant negative TLR5 allele have decreased inflammatory response to O3 exposure ex vivo.
source: We demonstrate that immune cells of human carriers of a dominant negative TLR5 allele have decreased inflammatory response to O3 exposure ex vivo and LPS exposure in vitro.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from human subjects shown in Figure 4.

claim: TLR5 physically associates with TLR4.
source: Using primary murine macrophages, we find that TLR5 physically associates with TLR4 and biases TLR4 signaling towards the MyD88 pathway.
evidence: This claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 8.

claim: TLR5 biases TLR4 signaling towards the MyD88 pathway.
source: Using primary murine macrophages, we find that TLR5 physically associates with TLR4 and biases TLR4 signaling towards the MyD88 pathway.
evidence: This claim is supported by data showing enhanced MyD88-dependent signaling in the presence of TLR5, as shown in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: In the US alone, over 15% of the population suffers from lung disease, at an annual cost of 120,000 deaths, and >$50 billion.
source: In the US alone, over 15% of the population suffers from lung disease, at an annual cost of 120,000 deaths, and >$50 billion (Redd, 2002; Kochanek et al., 2011; Ford et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published epidemiological data.

claim: Household LPS levels are directly associated with asthma symptoms and asthma-related health care utilization.
source: For example, household LPS levels are directly associated with asthma symptoms and asthma-related health care utilization (Thorne et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Thorne et al., 2005.

claim: For every 10 parts-per-billion (ppb) increase in O3 levels there is an associated mortality increase of 0.39–0.87%.
source: Also, sound epidemiological studies suggest that for every 10 parts-per-billion (ppb) increase in O3 levels there is an associated mortality increase of 0.39–0.87% (Katsouyanni et al., 1995; Levy et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to epidemiological studies.

claim: TLR4 is the prototypic receptor for LPS.
source: TLR4 is the prototypic receptor for LPS (Kawai and Akira, 2010), which is found in particulate-matter pollution and house dust (Thorne et al., 2005; Mueller-Anneling et al., 2004) and is a major contributor to sepsis-induced lung injury (Andonegui et al., 2003; Baumgarten et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Kawai and Akira, 2010.

claim: TLR4 can heterodimerize with other TLR like TLR2 and TLR6.
source: TLR4 can heterodimerize with other TLR like TLR2 and TLR6 (Stewart et al., 2010; Wang et al., 2014); in these cases, the partner TLRs serve to expand the TLR4 ligand spectrum.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Stewart et al., 2010 and Wang et al., 2014.

claim: TLR4-TLR5 interaction has been reported once, wherein TLR4 was shown to promote nitric oxide production after flagellin exposure.
source: TLR4-TLR5 interaction has been reported once (Mizel et al., 2003), wherein TLR4 was shown to promote nitric oxide production after flagellin exposure.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Mizel et al., 2003.

claim: TLR5 is induced after injury.
source: TLR5, the prototypic receptor for bacterial flagellin, is expressed in alveolar macrophages (Shikhagaie et al., 2014), is induced after injury (Menendez et al., 2011) and regulates the immune response to injury (Burdelya et al., 2008; Uematsu et al., 2008; Wilson et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Menendez et al., 2011.

claim: Known functional genetic polymorphisms in TLR5 are associated with susceptibility to infections.
source: Furthermore, known functional genetic polymorphisms in TLR5 are associated with susceptibility to infections (Hawn et al., 2003; Grube et al., 2013; West et al., 2013) and autoimmune disease (Gewirtz et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies on TLR5 polymorphisms.

claim: TLR5 deficiency in mice significantly alters the in vivo response to TLR4 activators LPS, hyaluronan and O3.
source: We show that TLR5 deficiency in mice significantly alters the in vivo response to TLR4 activators LPS, hyaluronan and O3.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from multiple in vivo models shown in Figures 1, 2, and 3.

claim: After ultrapure LPS exposure, TLR5 co-immunoprecipitates with MyD88, TLR4 and LPS.
source: Mechanistically, we show that after ultrapure LPS exposure, TLR5 co-immunoprecipitates with MyD88, TLR4 and LPS.
evidence: This claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figures 6 and 8.

claim: The presence of TLR5 promotes formation of the Myddosome, that is association of MyD88 and IRAK4.
source: The presence of TLR5 promotes formation of the Myddosome, that is association of MyD88 and IRAK4, and biases TLR4 signaling towards the MyD88 pathway.
evidence: This claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data showing decreased IRAK4-MyD88 association in TLR5-deficient cells, as shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Human carriers of a dominant-negative TLR5 allele have decreased inflammatory response to LPS exposure in vitro.
source: Finally, we demonstrate that human carriers of a dominant-negative TLR5 allele have decreased inflammatory response to O3 exposure in vivo and LPS exposure in vitro.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from human monocyte-derived macrophages shown in Figure 4A.

claim: LPS exposure led to substantial lung inflammation in wildtype mice, which was ameliorated in the absence of TLR5.
source: As expected, this led to substantial lung inflammation in wildtype mice, which was ameliorated in the absence of TLR5 (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by histological data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: TLR5 deficiency ameliorated cellular influx and lung injury as evidenced by lung lavage protein.
source: TLR5 deficiency also ameliorated cellular influx and lung injury as evidenced by lung lavage protein (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Expression of inflammatory cytokines in the lung was significantly ameliorated in Tlr5-deficient mice after LPS exposure.
source: Furthermore, expression of inflammatory cytokines in the lung was significantly ameliorated in Tlr5-deficient mice (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-PCR and ELISA data shown in Figures 1C and 1D.

claim: Tlr5-deficient mice had ameliorated airway cytokine expression after O3 exposure.
source: Tlr5-deficient mice had ameliorated airway cytokine expression and almost abolished AHR after O3 exposure (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by cytokine measurement data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Tlr5-deficient mice had almost abolished AHR after O3 exposure.
source: Tlr5-deficient mice had ameliorated airway cytokine expression and almost abolished AHR after O3 exposure (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by airway physiology measurements shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Hyaluronan is the endogenous danger-associated molecular pattern that activates TLR4 and mediates the response after O3 exposure.
source: Because hyaluronan is the endogenous danger-associated molecular pattern that activates TLR4 and mediates the response after O3 exposure (Garantziotis et al., 2010; Garantziotis et al., 2009), we then investigated the effect of TLR5 on hyaluronan signaling.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Garantziotis et al., 2010; Garantziotis et al., 2009).

claim: Tlr5-deficient mice had substantially reduced inflammatory gene induction after hyaluronan exposure.
source: Tlr5-deficient mice had substantially reduced inflammatory gene induction and significantly diminished AHR after instilled ultrapure (pharmaceutical grade) hyaluronan exposure (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Tlr5-deficient mice had significantly diminished AHR after hyaluronan exposure.
source: Tlr5-deficient mice had substantially reduced inflammatory gene induction and significantly diminished AHR after instilled ultrapure (pharmaceutical grade) hyaluronan exposure (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by airway physiology measurements shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Deficiency in Tlr4, Tlr5, or Myd88 abolished the tracheal ring response to hyaluronan.
source: We found that deficiency in either of the 3 molecules abolished the response to hyaluronan (Figure 3C) suggesting that TLR4 and TLR5 are non-redundant and necessary for the hyaluronan-MyD88 signaling response.
evidence: This claim is supported by tracheal ring constriction measurements shown in Figure 3C.

claim: TLR4 and TLR5 are non-redundant and necessary for the hyaluronan-MyD88 signaling response.
source: We found that deficiency in either of the 3 molecules abolished the response to hyaluronan (Figure 3C) suggesting that TLR4 and TLR5 are non-redundant and necessary for the hyaluronan-MyD88 signaling response.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing that deficiency in either TLR4 or TLR5 abolishes the response, as shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The presence or absence of functional TLR5 is associated with differential regulation of immune genes.
source: We showed that the presence or absence of functional TLR5 is associated with differential regulation of immune genes in this panel.
evidence: This claim is supported by NanoString gene expression analysis data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: There was a linear correlation between the magnitude of the TLR5 effect and the proportion of genes that are either published or predicted to be downstream of the NFκB pathway.
source: Interestingly, there was a linear correlation between the magnitude of the TLR5 effect and the proportion of genes that are either published or predicted to be downstream of the NFκB pathway (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C): among the genes that were 70–90% upregulated in Tlr5-sufficient mice compared to Tlr5-deficient mice, almost 90% were in the NFκB pathway, while this proportion fell to 50% among the genes that were not different between genotypes. (R2 = 0.89, p=0.0013).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of gene expression data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C.

claim: TLR5 preferentially impacts gene expression downstream of NFκB activation.
source: This may suggest that TLR5 preferentially impacts gene expression downstream of NFκB activation.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on the correlation observed in the gene expression data.

claim: A dominant-negative TLR5 single nucleotide polymorphism (rs5744168, TLR5392STOP) is found with a prevalence of 8–10% in Caucasians and 3% in African Americans.
source: In humans, a dominant-negative TLR5 single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) (rs5744168, TLR5392STOP) (Hawn et al., 2003) is found with a prevalence of 8–10% in Caucasians and 3% in African Americans.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Hawn et al., 2003.

claim: Whole blood from rs5744168 minor-allele carriers does not differ in the response to LPS compared to 'wildtype'.
source: Others have reported that whole blood from rs5744168 minor-allele carriers does not differ in the response to LPS compared to 'wildtype' (West et al., 2013), and we confirmed this finding (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to West et al., 2013 and confirmed by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Macrophages from rs5744168 minor-allele carriers had a decreased response to flagellin and ultrapure LPS, but not Pam3CSK4.
source: Macrophages from rs5744168 minor-allele carriers had a decreased response to flagellin and ultrapure LPS, but not Pam3CSK4 (Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), thus confirming that human TLR5 genetic variation specifically determines the response to LPS.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from human monocyte-derived macrophages shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Human TLR5 genetic variation specifically determines the response to LPS.
source: Macrophages from rs5744168 minor-allele carriers had a decreased response to flagellin and ultrapure LPS, but not Pam3CSK4 (Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), thus confirming that human TLR5 genetic variation specifically determines the response to LPS.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the specificity of the response to LPS and flagellin but not Pam3CSK4 in carriers of the TLR5 polymorphism.

claim: The decreased response to LPS in rs5744168 carriers was not due to altered expression of TLR4 or CD14.
source: This was not due to altered expression of TLR4 or CD14, which was not changed by the rs5744168 genotype (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: TLR5 expression was modestly increased in alveolar macrophages of human volunteers after O3 exposure.
source: TLR5 expression was modestly increased in alveolar macrophages of human volunteers after O3 exposure (Figure 4B, p=0.05 by Wilcoxon pairwise signed rank test).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-PCR data from human alveolar macrophages shown in Figure 4B.

claim: TNFα expression by alveolar macrophages after O3 exposure was not increased in any of the TLR5-deficient individuals (rs5744168 minor-allele carriers), while it was increased in wildtype-allele carriers.
source: We found, that TNFα expression by alveolar macrophages after O3 exposure was not increased in any of the TLR5-deficient individuals (rs5744168 minor-allele carriers), while it was increased in wildtype-allele carriers (Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by TNFα measurement data from human alveolar macrophages shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Tlr5-deficient BMDM had significantly decreased expression of TNFα and IL-6 after ultrapure LPS exposure in vitro, by an average of 30–50%.
source: Tlr5-deficient BMDM had significantly decreased expression of TNFα and IL-6 after ultrapure LPS exposure in vitro, by an average of 30–50% (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by ELISA data from murine BMDMs shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Tlr4-deficient BMDM showed no response to ultrapure LPS.
source: To ensure that the altered response was not due to LPS contaminants despite the ultrapure preparation, we also assayed Tlr4-deficient BMDM and saw no response to ultrapure LPS (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by ELISA data from Tlr4-deficient BMDMs shown in Figure 5A.

claim: RAW264.7 cells are naturally deficient in Tlr5.
source: To ascertain that our observation was not due to an off-target effect of genetic Tlr5 ablation on macrophage biology, we used RAW264.7 cells, a murine macrophage cell line, which are naturally deficient in Tlr5 (McDonald et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to McDonald et al., 2007.

claim: Tlr5-transfected RAW264.7 cells had significantly higher TNFα expression in response to ultrapure LPS compared to non-transfected cells.
source: We transfected these cells with a murine Tlr5 construct, or empty vector, and noted that the Tlr5-transfected cells had significantly higher TNFα expression in response to ultrapure LPS (and the TLR5 ligand flagellin, as expected).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from transfected RAW264.7 cells shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The TLR5-dependent effect was specific to LPS exposure, as responses to poly(I:C) (TLR3 ligand), Pam3CSK4 (TLR2 ligand), and ODN (TLR9 ligand) were not affected by the presence of TLR5.
source: The TLR5-dependent effect was specific to LPS exposure, as responses to poly(I:C) (TLR3 ligand), Pam3CSK4 (TLR2 ligand), and ODN (TLR9 ligand) were not affected by the presence of TLR5 (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from transfected RAW264.7 cells exposed to various TLR ligands, shown in Figure 5B.

claim: TLR4 signals through both MyD88 and TRIF pathways.
source: TLR4 signals through both MyD88 and TRIF pathways, whereas TLR5 is so far only known to signal through MyD88 (Kawai and Akira, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Kawai and Akira, 2010.

claim: TLR5 is so far only known to signal through MyD88.
source: TLR4 signals through both MyD88 and TRIF pathways, whereas TLR5 is so far only known to signal through MyD88 (Kawai and Akira, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Kawai and Akira, 2010.

claim: In primary murine and human BMDMs, MyD88 co-immunoprecipitated with TLR5 after ultrapure LPS exposure.
source: We found that, in primary murine and human BMDMs, MyD88 co-immunoprecipitated with TLR5 after ultrapure LPS exposure (Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The association of TLR5 with MyD88 was directly dependent upon TLR4 activation, since it was not observed in Tlr4-deficient primary BMDM.
source: This association was directly dependent upon TLR4 activation, since it was not observed in Tlr4-deficient primary BMDM (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data from Tlr4-deficient BMDMs shown in Figure 6B.

claim: TLR4 immunoprecipitated with MyD88 after LPS exposure.
source: TLR4, as expected, also immunoprecipitated with MyD88 after LPS exposure (Figure 6B, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The association of MyD88 with TLR4 and TLR5 was specific, since other TLR like TLR6 and TLR7 did not immunoprecipitate with MyD88 after LPS exposure.
source: Furthermore, the association of MyD88 with TLR4 and TLR5 was specific, since other TLR like TLR6 and TLR7 did not immunoprecipitate with MyD88 after LPS exposure (Figure 6B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data showing lack of association with TLR6 and TLR7, shown in Figure 6B and C.

claim: MyD88 signaling occurs through the complexing of Myd88 with IRAK-4 which stabilizes formation of the so-called Myddosome.
source: MyD88 signaling occurs through the complexing of Myd88 with IRAK-4 which stabilizes formation of the so-called Myddosome (Gay et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Gay et al., 2011.

claim: Tlr5-deficient BMDM had decreased immunoprecipitation of IRAK-4 with MyD88.
source: Tlr5-deficient BMDM had decreased immunoprecipitation of IRAK-4 with MyD88 (Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: There was significant reduction in the phosphorylation of IKKα/β, IκB, p65, JNK1/2 and ERK1/2 in Tlr5-deficient BMDMs compared with wildtype cells during early activation.
source: There was also significant reduction in the phosphorylation of IKKα/β, IκB, p65, JNK1/2 and ERK1/2 in Tlr5-deficient BMDMs compared with wildtype cells during early activation (Figure 7A,B, Figure 7—figure supplement 1A), which is MyD88- but not TRIF-dependent (Kawai et al., 2001; Yamamoto et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 7A,B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Phosphorylation of IKKα/β, IκB, p65, JNK1/2 and ERK1/2 is MyD88- but not TRIF-dependent.
source: There was also significant reduction in the phosphorylation of IKKα/β, IκB, p65, JNK1/2 and ERK1/2 in Tlr5-deficient BMDMs compared with wildtype cells during early activation (Figure 7A,B, Figure 7—figure supplement 1A), which is MyD88- but not TRIF-dependent (Kawai et al., 2001; Yamamoto et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kawai et al., 2001 and Yamamoto et al., 2003.

claim: Nuclear IRF3 (a specific readout of TRIF-dependent signaling) was not affected in Tlr5-deficient cells.
source: Nuclear IRF3 (a specific readout of TRIF-dependent signaling Honda and Taniguchi, 2006) was not affected in Tlr5-deficient cells (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claim: TLR5 directly interacts with MyD88 after LPS exposure and enhances MyD88-dependent TLR4 signaling by promoting efficient assembly of Myddosome.
source: In aggregate, these results support that TLR5 directly interacts with MyD88 after LPS exposure and enhances MyD88-dependent TLR4 signaling by promoting efficient assembly of Myddosome.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the collective experimental data showing TLR5-MyD88 interaction and enhanced Myddosome formation.

claim: There were no differences in basal levels of cell surface TLR4 or CD14 between Tlr5-deficient and –sufficient BMDM.
source: There were no differences in basal levels of cell surface TLR4 or CD14 between Tlr5-deficient and –sufficient BMDM, nor in LPS-induced internalization of TLR4 (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1A–D.

claim: There were no differences in LPS-induced internalization of TLR4 between Tlr5-deficient and –sufficient BMDM.
source: There were no differences in basal levels of cell surface TLR4 or CD14 between Tlr5-deficient and –sufficient BMDM, nor in LPS-induced internalization of TLR4 (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1A–D.

claim: TLR4 and TLR5 reciprocally co-immunoprecipitated in transfected HEK293 cells.
source: Because we were unable to find commercially available validated antibodies against TLR4 that could be used in co-immunoprecipitation experiments, we utilized an induced expression system using tagged TLR4 and TLR5 in HEK293 cells and found that TLR4 and TLR5 reciprocally co-immunoprecipitated in transfected HEK293 cells (Figure 8A).
evidence: This claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data from transfected HEK293 cells shown in Figure 8A.

claim: TLR4 and TLR5 interact as confirmed by Proximity Ligation Assay in HeLa cells.
source: We then overexpressed TLR4 and TLR5 in HeLa cells and confirmed their interaction through a Proximity Ligation Assay (Figure 8—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by Proximity Ligation Assay data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1E.

claim: TLR5 co-precipitates with biotin-tagged LPS in TLR5-hemagglutinin tagged expressing RAW264.7 cells.
source: Furthermore, we exposed TLR5-hemagglutinin tagged expressing RAW264.7 cells to biotin-tagged LPS, and (after thoroughly washing the cells) could co-precipitate TLR5 with LPS (Figure 8B).
evidence: This claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: TLR5 directly participates in the TLR4 signaling complex after LPS exposure.
source: These results suggest that TLR5 directly participates in the TLR4 signaling complex after LPS exposure, and, in aggregate, support a functional interaction of TLR5 with TLR4 in the response to environmental injury.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the collective experimental data showing TLR5-TLR4 interaction and co-precipitation with LPS.

claim: TLR5 heteromerization with TLR4 modulates canonical TLR4 signaling and promotes activation of the MyD88 pathway.
source: The important novel finding from our work, is that TLR5 heteromerization with TLR4 modulates canonical TLR4 signaling and promotes activation of the MyD88 pathway.
evidence: This claim is supported by the collective experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: CD14 controls TLR4 endocytosis after LPS ligation, and thus is necessary for TRIF signaling, which is thought to occur in the endosomal compartment.
source: For example, elegant work has demonstrated that CD14, which is necessary for LPS binding to TLR4, also controls TLR4 endocytosis after LPS ligation, and thus is necessary for TRIF signaling, which is thought to occur in the endosomal compartment (Zanoni et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Zanoni et al., 2011.

claim: TLR5 does not regulate LPS-induced internalization of TLR4.
source: Unlike CD14, TLR5 does not appear to regulate LPS-induced internalization of TLR4 (Figure 8—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1C.

claim: TLR5 promotes TLR4/MyD88 signaling at the plasma membrane by enhancing the assembly of the Myddosome.
source: Our findings rather support a model in which TLR5 promotes TLR4/MyD88 signaling at the plasma membrane by enhancing the assembly of the Myddosome.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing enhanced Myddosome formation and MyD88-dependent signaling in the presence of TLR5.

claim: TLR5-deficient mice had approx. 30–50% decreased cytokine expression in local and systemic LPS models of lung inflammation.
source: TLR5-deficient mice had approx. 30–50% decreased cytokine expression in local and systemic LPS models of lung inflammation, while airway hyperresponsiveness after ozone or hyaluronan exposure was significantly reduced, and inflammatory gene induction after hyaluronan exposure was abolished.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from in vivo LPS models shown in Figures 1 and 5.

claim: Airway hyperresponsiveness after ozone or hyaluronan exposure was significantly reduced in TLR5-deficient mice.
source: TLR5-deficient mice had approx. 30–50% decreased cytokine expression in local and systemic LPS models of lung inflammation, while airway hyperresponsiveness after ozone or hyaluronan exposure was significantly reduced, and inflammatory gene induction after hyaluronan exposure was abolished.
evidence: This claim is supported by airway physiology data shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Inflammatory gene induction after hyaluronan exposure was abolished in TLR5-deficient mice.
source: TLR5-deficient mice had approx. 30–50% decreased cytokine expression in local and systemic LPS models of lung inflammation, while airway hyperresponsiveness after ozone or hyaluronan exposure was significantly reduced, and inflammatory gene induction after hyaluronan exposure was abolished.
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The 'fine-tuning', MyD88-promoting effects of TLR5 are particularly evident in lower-grade inflammation such as ozone- or hyaluronan-induced.
source: It is possible that the 'fine-tuning', MyD88-promoting effects of TLR5 are particularly evident in lower-grade inflammation such as ozone- or hyaluronan-induced, which explains the larger impact on TLR5 deficiency on human and murine inflammation after ozone exposure compared to LPS exposure.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on the observed differences in TLR5 effects across different models.

claim: The ability of the Myddosome to form 7:4 and 8:4 MyD88:IRAK4 stoichiometries is a potential mechanism through which clusters of activated TLR receptors can be formed and different TLR receptors can be recruited into the same assembly.
source: Indeed, it has been postulated that the ability of the Myddosome to form 7:4 and 8:4 MyD88:IRAK4 stoichiometries is a potential mechanism through which clusters of activated TLR receptors can be formed and different TLR receptors can be recruited into the same assembly (Motshwene et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Motshwene et al., 2009.

claim: Higher-order assembly of receptor complexes in lipid raft microdomains is likely to be crucial in the fine-regulation of immune responses.
source: Higher-order assembly of receptor complexes in lipid raft microdomains is likely to be crucial in the fine-regulation of immune responses (Gay et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Gay et al., 2011.

claim: TLR5 may be part of the higher-order receptor assembly that regulates TLR4 signaling.
source: Our work suggests that TLR5 may be part of the higher-order receptor assembly that regulates TLR4 signaling.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing TLR5 participation in the TLR4 signaling complex.

claim: Until now, the effect of TLR4 heteromerization has always been to expand the TLR4 ligand spectrum.
source: TLR4 is a promiscuous receptor, having been found to heterodimerize with TLR2 and TLR6 (Stewart et al., 2010; Wang et al., 2014) but the effect of heteromerization until now has always been to expand the TLR4 ligand spectrum.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Stewart et al., 2010 and Wang et al., 2014.

claim: This is the first work to demonstrate that TLR heteromerization may serve to modulate canonical TLR signaling.
source: To our knowledge, this is the first work to demonstrate that TLR heteromerization may serve to modulate canonical TLR signaling.
evidence: This claim is based on the novelty of the findings presented in this manuscript.

claim: TLR5 heteromerization with TLR4 may help recruit additional MyD88 moieties to the signaling complex, and thus promote downstream signaling.
source: TLR5 heteromerization with TLR4 may help recruit additional MyD88 moieties to the signaling complex, and thus promote downstream signaling.
evidence: This claim is speculative, proposing a mechanism for the observed effects.

claim: Endogenous activators of both TLR4 and TLR5, like hyaluronan or HMGB1, may engage these receptors and promote the signaling response.
source: Alternatively, or perhaps in addition, endogenous activators of both TLR4 and TLR5, like hyaluronan or HMGB1 (Das et al., 2016) may engage these receptors and promote the signaling response.
evidence: This claim is speculative, proposing an alternative mechanism, and is supported by citation to Das et al., 2016.

claim: A recent paper supported the role of TLR5 in TLR4 signaling, showing similar effects of the rs5744168 minor allele polymorphism on TNFα and IL-8 expression by human monocytes after LPS exposure.
source: A recent paper supported the role or TLR5 in TLR4 signaling, showing similar effects of the rs5744168 minor allele polymorphism on TNFα and IL-8 expression by human monocytes after LPS exposure, and also demonstrating that TLR5 does not influence the gene expression of TLR4 (45), as we also show.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to another study (reference 45, which is Dickey et al., 2019).

claim: The current model of canonical TLR4 activation rather applies to the TLR5 deficient status.
source: In summary, our results suggest a new model of TLR4-TLR5 complex formation in response to the PAMP LPS or the DAMP hyaluronan (Figure 9). We propose that the hitherto accepted model of TLR4 signaling through pure TLR4 homodimers rather reflects the TLR5-deficient state.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the collective experimental findings and is illustrated in Figure 9.

claim: In TLR5-expressing cells, TLR5 participates in a heteromeric higher-order TLR4 receptor complex and potentiates MyD88 signaling by promoting efficient assembly of the Myddosome.
source: In TLR5-expressing cells, TLR5 participates in a heteromeric higher-order TLR4 receptor complex and potentiates MyD88 signaling by promoting efficient assembly of the Myddosome.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the collective experimental data and is illustrated in Figure 9.

claim: Exposures that induce TLR5 expression, such as DNA injury, p53 activation or flagellated bacterial infection may in parallel prime the MyD88-dependent pro-inflammatory response to LPS.
source: This may suggest that exposures that induce TLR5 expression, such as DNA injury, p53 activation (Menendez et al., 2011) or flagellated bacterial infection may in parallel prime the MyD88-dependent pro-inflammatory response to LPS, due to the presence of more TLR5 receptors which may promote TLR4 signaling.
evidence: This claim is speculative, proposing a broader implication of the findings, and is supported by citation to Menendez et al., 2011.

claim: In a finite TLR4 receptor pool the presence of TLR5/TLR4 higher-order complexes would bias TLR4 signaling towards MyD88.
source: Since TLR5 signals through MyD88, in a finite TLR4 receptor pool the presence of TLR5/TLR4 higher-order complexes would bias TLR4 signaling towards MyD88.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data and the known signaling properties of TLR5.

claim: Cell surface expression of TLR4 on immune cells is low (a few hundred or thousand molecules per cell) compared to other TLRs.
source: Notably, cell surface expression of TLR4 on immune cells is low (a few hundred or thousand molecules per cell) compared to other TLRs (Visintin et al., 2001; Juarez et al., 2010), supporting that the presence of relatively few TLR5 receptor molecules may suffice to augment MyD88 signaling downstream of TLR4.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Visintin et al., 2001 and Juarez et al., 2010.
